articles.title: Sheffield's Niche club to return to city dancefloors
articles.summary: Niche, which opened on Sidney Street in 1992, is credited with the birth of 'bassline' music.
articles.body:
A renowned Sheffield nightclub which became synonymous with the birth of 'bassline' music is making a comeback.

Niche originally opened in a former cutlery warehouse on Sidney Street in 1992 and grew from an underground spot to become one of the most influential names in UK club culture.

A number of incidents involving drugs and violence culminated in greater police scrutiny and the original premises closed in 2005 after a large police raid. Despite several relocations across the city, Niche closed permanently in 2018 after more stabbings outside the club.

Now under new ownership, Niche is being developed as a contemporary music and cultural brand, with a new club night on 17 October.

Steve Baxendale, the former owner of Niche, passed away aged 67 in 2019. His wife Helen has now passed ownership of the brand to a new Sheffield-based team with previous experience in music, DJing and club promotion.

New operations director Drew Garber said they wanted to build the name into "Sheffield super-brand the city can be proud of".

"People care deeply about Niche and we know our responsibility is to keep that legacy in safe hands while giving the residents and artists who built it a home, and the next generation a genuine platform," he added.

Niche was part of a club scene in Sheffield in the 90s along with Gatecrasher One/Republic located nearby in a converted former steelworks warehouse, that transformed the city into a powerhouse for electronic music, rave culture, and super clubs drawing visitors from across the UK and abroad.

In its heyday, Niche's resident DJs like Jamie Duggan played speed garage and house with heavy low-end basslines and shuffling hi-hats , producing a sound that became known as 'bassline' or simply Niche.

Live sets recorded inside the club, known as the "Niche Tapes" were sold far beyond Sheffield, building a national audience and turning the name from a venue into a wider cultural brand.

The club did however begin to garner a reputation for violence and gang culture. Former manager Michael Baxendale, brother of former owner Steve, died after being stabbed outside the venue.

Four men were later jailed after their involvement in a mass brawl at the club after it moved to Walker Street near the Wicker. The club closed shortly afterwards.

Speaking to the BBC in 2014, Assistant Chief Constable Paul Broadbent said: "We needed to take some positive police action on a nightclub where guns had been seen and fired. Class A, serious illegal drugs had been seen, sold, used and supplied.

"Criminal gangs from Manchester, Leeds, Leicester and other cities were coming to the Niche to do their business. I'm not allowing that to happen in Sheffield."

New owner Fraser Rowlin acknowledged the club's past reputation but said the scene had "come a long way".

"Obviously, the history is there and it kind of blew up but we are 30 years on now.

"We have moved towards making sure clubs and events we put on are as safe as possible using every form of technology we can.

"The whole nature of that genre has changed. It's not as gritty and dark as it used to be. It's transcended that now."

The return of Niche begins with a night at Network Sheffield, which the owners described as a "homecoming".

articles.title: Beyoncé's beauty brand is expanding its scholarship fund to the UK; 10 schools will receive $250,000 to train the next generation of hair professionals
articles.summary: Beyoncé’s haircare business is extending its support for aspiring hair professionals beyond the United States, bringing its scholarship programme to the
articles.body: Beyoncé’s haircare business is extending its support for aspiring hair professionals beyond the United States, bringing its scholarship programme to the United Kingdom for the first time. Reportedly, the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund has committed $250,000 to cosmetology and barbering education in 2026, with 10 schools set to receive $25,000 each. The funding is intended to help students cover tuition and other education-related costs as they prepare for careers in the beauty industry. The latest round doubles the number of participating schools from the previous five, building on a programme that has supported both students and salon owners since 2024.Beyoncé’s Cécred scholarship fund expands to 10 schools with its first UK partnershipsThe Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund is increasing the number of educational institutions involved in its scholarship programme from five to 10 in 2026. The new intake also extends beyond the United States, with schools in the United Kingdom becoming part of the initiative for the first time since its launch in 2024.The fund has allocated $250,000 to this year's education programme. Each of the 10 selected institutions will receive $25,000 to support students studying cosmetology and barbering. The money is intended to help cover tuition and other education-related expenses, giving participating schools funding to direct towards students preparing for careers in the hair industry.The expansion builds on a programme that has previously operated in several US markets. Its move into the UK gives the fund an international presence, although the published announcement does not identify the 10 participating schools individually.How the fund supports students entering the hair industryThe scholarship programme is part of a broader effort to support the people who work in salons and barbershops, including those still completing their training. Students need practical experience alongside their classroom education, and the costs associated with professional courses can include supplies and other materials required to develop technical skills.By directing funding through partner institutions, the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund can contribute towards these expenses without limiting its support to established professionals. The 2026 allocation is dedicated to education, rather than being divided between students and existing business owners as it was during the fund's first year.Tina Knowles, chair of the BeyGOOD Foundation's board and vice chairwoman at Cécred described, “We strive to uplift the professional hair industry and grow the salon community, while giving students and salon owners the tools they need to progress it forward.”The programme began with a $500,000 investment in 2024When the Cécred x BeyGOOD Fund launched in 2024, it committed $500,000 to supporting salon professionals and students. The initial programme covered five US states: California, Georgia, Illinois, New Jersey and Texas.Education received half of that first investment, amounting to $250,000. Twenty-five cosmetology students at five partner schools were awarded scholarships worth $10,000 each. The remaining $250,000 went to 25 salon and barbershop owners, who also received $10,000 apiece to help maintain or develop their businesses.That first round established the fund's two main areas of support. It addressed the training costs faced by people entering the profession while also offering financial assistance to those already running businesses in the sector.Beyoncé’s fund supported 37 salon owners and 46 students in 2025The fund widened its reach across the United States in 2025, maintaining its total investment at $500,000. Its support for established businesses grew, with $370,000 distributed among 37 salon and barbershop owners in grants of $10,000 each.Those recipients also had access to business development assistance, mentoring and other resources through a partnership with the National Minority Supplier Development Council (NMSDC). The arrangement extended the programme beyond direct grants by connecting owners with support intended to help them manage and develop their businesses.Students continued to receive funding that year, although the education allocation was smaller than in the inaugural round. A total of $130,000 was set aside for scholarships awarded to 46 cosmetology and barbering students.The 2026 programme takes a different approach. Rather than repeating the previous year's split between business grants and student scholarships, the announced $250,000 investment is focused on education. Doubling the number of participating schools and adding the UK gives the latest round a wider institutional reach, even as its total funding is lower than the $500,000 commitments made in each of the two preceding years.Cécred’s beauty business and BeyGOOD’s charitable workCécred is Beyoncé's haircare brand, while BeyGOOD is the philanthropic organisation associated with the singer. Their joint fund brings the two together around an industry in which training, technical knowledge and small-business ownership are closely linked.Salon professionals often build their careers through formal education followed by practical work, and some eventually establish businesses of their own. The fund's earlier rounds reflected both stages, with scholarships for students and grants for salon and barbershop owners. Its latest allocation places greater emphasis on the training stage, with schools serving as the route through which financial assistance will reach students.For 2026, the immediate commitment is clear: 10 institutions will receive $25,000 each, bringing the total education investment to $250,000. The inclusion of UK schools extends the programme beyond its original American base. Which institutions will take part, and how the individual schools will distribute the funding, remain details to be confirmed in the published announcement.You use AI every day. articles.title: Unseen Vivienne Westwood photos show 'born protester'
articles.summary: Images of the fashion icon's fracking protest show "the reality of her", Paul Wolfgang Webster says.
articles.body:
From Alan Bennett to Sir Alex Ferguson, Betty Boothroyd to Bez and Fred Dibnah to Iain Duncan Smith, Paul Wolfgang Webster has photographed a wide range of well-known faces across his decades-long career, but one eluded him.

As a punk, he always wanted to capture an icon of the scene, Dame Vivienne Westwood, but never had the opportunity.

That was until the fashion legend turned up at an anti-fracking protest in Lancashire in 2018.

Discussing the event ahead of an exhibition of his unseen photographs from that day, Wolfgang said the encounter was everything he had always hoped it would be, adding: "It was like she was Joan of Arc, walking down the street with this big crusade of people behind her."

The fashion designer, who grew up on the outskirts of the Derbyshire town of Glossop in the 1940s and 50s before moving to London in her teens, became almost as well-known for her activism as she was for her couture.

Alongside her work in fashion, she campaigned relentlessly on the causes she held dear.

She supported Aids Research, Peta and Oxfam, gave hundreds of thousands to the Green Party and was a regular visitor to Wikileaks co-founder Julian Assange during his seven years in the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

She even parked a white tank outside then-Prime Minister David Cameron's house in a protest against fracking, part of a campaign that later brought her to Little Plumpton in Lancashire in October 2018, after the site was earmarked for fracking.

It was an opportunity that Wolfgang could not pass up.

Dame Vivienne Westwood - the godmother of punk

Vivienne Westwood: Buy less, choose well

"The punk era itself came about because of politics at that time and... Vivienne's punk design came from that.

"I've also had an affinity with that in my own work.

"When I found out she was going to the protest, I knew that was my chance."

The 62-year-old said the day gave him a behind-the-scenes glimpse of the "real" Westwood and what he captured showed the "born protester" stringing together banners, making tea for the campaigners and doing a dissenting dance to Abba's Dancing Queen.

"I wanted to photograph what she was doing as a record of that day," said Wolfgang.

"She didn't drive around in big black limousines with security, like A-listers do.

"She was there helping out and setting up everything."

He said seeing her lead a march was nothing short of spectacular.

"It was like she was Joan of Arc walking down the street with this big crusade of people behind her.

"It was quite a spectacle just watching her."

The day also gave him the chance to speak with Westwood, a chat which showed him exactly why she was such a beloved figure.

"She starting speaking to me like she'd known me all my life," he said.

"[We spoke] about the cut of the recent royal wedding dress, about my wife who had worn one of her dresses at our wedding.

"She was very open and very approachable.

"It was a beautiful conversation - she was the woman I had always hoped she was."

Wolfgang said the Abba dance was a rebellious nod to then-PM Theresa May, who had danced her way on stage to the same tune at a recent Conservative Party conference , and part of Westwood's subversive way of challenging the establishment.

"By dancing to the Abba track, she was saying sometimes there's nothing done by politicians," he said.

"She was actually using it to demonstrate 'I'm not gonna just sit here and do nothing'.

He said that for him, the moment encapsulated the approach Westwood, who died aged 81 in 2022 , took to her life and career.

"She never let go of standing for her values about changing the world and something, which in her eyes, was for the better," he said.

"She was 77 then but she was there, protesting basically until the day she died.

"She was a born protester [and] she carried her connection to the North West with her for all of her life."

He said his collection of photographs, which will be shown for the first time, gave "an insight to how she works".

"We read about her and see pictures and everything, but this is showing quite an intimate side to that.

"It is her in her zone, talking to people, working on something she believed in.

The Westwood-led day of protest was far from the only campaigning at the site.

The site on Preston New Road, near Blackpool, was the country's first horizontal fracking site but after more than 120 tremors were recorded during drilling, the controversial process was banned in 2019.

Fracking - a process which involves drilling into the earth and directing a high-pressure mixture of water, sand and chemicals at a rock layer, to release the gas inside - sparked lengthy protests from environmentalist groups and local communities in Lancashire.

The drilling site was suspended for a final time in 2022.

Wolfgang said the serendipitous matching of that date with his show felt "poignant".

"It will be a 'full circle' moment to see the land restored by the closing date of the exhibition," he said.

Vivienne Westwood - Unseen Photography Exhibition by Paul Wolfgang Webster is at Manchester Central Library from 12 October to 31 December 2026. Entry is free.

articles.title: 'Edited version, if you have the courage, release entire video': CJP's Abhijeet Dipke
articles.summary: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has accused Delhi Police of denying him basic rights during his detention
articles.body: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has accused Delhi Police of denying him basic rights during his detention and demanded the release of the full video showing him repeatedly asking to be allowed to speak to his cousin and lawyer.According to news agency PTI, Dipke alleged that police had released an edited version of the video and challenged them to make the entire footage public so people could understand his account of the incident.“Delhi Police, if you have the courage, release the entire video in which I repeatedly asked them to let me speak to my cousin, give me my phone for two minutes and allow me to speak to my lawyer. Why are you not releasing that video? You are showing an edited version,” he said.“If you have the courage, show the entire video so that people can understand how you denied me my basic rights,” Dipke added.He claimed that police did not allow him to contact his lawyer after his arrest or detention, describing it as a violation of his legal rights. He also alleged that neither he nor his parents and lawyers were informed about where he was being held or which police station he had been taken to.“Allowing a person to call their lawyer after arrest or detention is a legal right. Delhi Police did not even allow me that, and now they are taking the moral high ground,” Dipke told news agency PTI.Dipke further alleged that police did not inform his family or lawyers about his whereabouts throughout the day.“They did not tell me, my parents or my lawyers where I was being held, which police station I was in or where in the country I had been taken. They did not inform anyone throughout the day,” he said.Dipke also accused Delhi Police of causing distress to his family by asking him to call his parents at 3.30am. He said his family had already been grieving the death of his grandmother.“At 3.30 am, they deliberately wanted me to call my parents and cause them further distress when they had already lost my grandmother. Was I supposed to give them another shock by telling them that their son was going to be jailed for a long time?” he asked.Alleging that the police action had caused mental distress to both him and his family, Dipke questioned why officers had repeatedly asked him to speak to his parents without informing them about his whereabouts.“Delhi Police was mentally torturing not just me but my family as well. Did the Delhi Police tell my family where I was being held? They kept telling me to speak to my parents, but did they tell my parents which jail or police station I was in? If they did not, why not? Why did they not tell them? Did they have no humanity?” he said.Meanwhile, CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ratna Singh are set to visit Parliament Street Police Station on Monday to seek permission for another peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar.The leaders will demand that Delhi Police allot a date and venue for the proposed demonstration within 24 hours, Ranka said.He warned that the party would announce another protest if the police failed to provide a date for the demonstration within the stipulated period.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: Drumcree dispute: Orangemen and Garvaghy residents both back in court
articles.summary: It follows a decision on Friday by the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to ban the march, after receiving police advice.
articles.body:
The Drumcree parading dispute is back in front of judges on Monday, with Portadown Orangemen and Garvaghy Road residents involved in separate court cases.

It follows a decision on Friday by the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to ban the march , after receiving police advice.

While the move has eased the immediate security situation, the issue remains unresolved.

Both sides have sought court interventions from differing perspectives.

Portadown Orangemen are seeking permission to challenge the secretary of state's decision to ban the parade on a number of grounds.

They include the police assessment of the situation.

An emergency hearing took place at Belfast High Court on Saturday, but it was adjourned until Monday.

The Court of Appeal is also set to rule on Monday whether the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition can contest the original Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.

Although Sir Chris subsequently banned it, he did not "strike down" the commission's ruling, which still stands.

The court heard arguments in the case last week.

A lawyer for the residents' group claimed the commission's decision was flawed over how it weighed up the potential for disorder if the parade was permitted.

The parade, by 35 members of Portadown District Orange Lodge, was meant to have gone ahead on 27 September.

However, an unlawful protest blocked the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and a two-week stand-off developed.

On Friday, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher urged the Secretary of State to intervene.

Boutcher said "proportionate options" to police the parade had been "exhausted" and any operation to clear the route would have "catastrophic" consequences.

Policing the stand-off has cost around £5m, largely due to officer overtime.

articles.body: One second, a man is sitting on a motorcycle. The next, the bike is caught in a violent collision, and he appears to escape just in time. A CCTV clip from Tuticorin has left social media users stunned, with many struggling to believe how quickly the scene unfolds. The moment looks almost like something from a film, but the danger behind it is very real.The moment that has everyone replaying the footageThe reported incident involves a speeding car crashing into a two-wheeler and sending it flying. The man on the motorcycle appears to move out of the way moments before the impact. While the bike suffers extensive damage, he reportedly escapes without serious injury.It is the suddenness of the collision that makes the footage so startling. There is barely any time to process what is happening before the motorcycle is thrown out of place.‘Where did the vehicle go?’That question has become the spirit of the online reaction. One user joked about the vehicle seemingly disappearing, while another remarked that the man had escaped by barely half an inch.Some compared the incident to an unbelievable movie scene. One user even invoked Newton’s first law of motion, adding a scientific reference to the flood of jokes.The humour reflects viewers’ disbelief, but it also shows how quickly a dangerous real-life incident can turn into online entertainment.Not everyone found the clip funnySeveral users questioned the motorcycle’s position on the road. Some argued that vehicles should not be parked or left standing in unsafe places, while others criticised the focus on punchlines instead of road safety.These reactions point to an important distinction. Unsafe stopping or parking can create hazards, but the available footage alone cannot establish every detail of what led to the crash. Nor does the position of a two-wheeler make speeding or careless driving acceptable.Why a split-second can change everythingA collision happens faster than most people can react. Drivers need enough time and distance to notice a hazard, respond and slow down. Speed reduces that margin for error and can make the consequences of a crash far more severe.The man's apparent escape may look extraordinary, but it should not be mistaken for a reliable way to avoid an accident. A person standing or sitting near a moving vehicle cannot always predict its path or move out of danger in time.A viral moment with a serious lessonThe missing-bike jokes may be what draw viewers to the clip, but the lasting takeaway should be different. Roads leave little room for mistakes, and a collision that ends without an obvious serious injury can easily have a different outcome.The footage has given the internet an astonishing moment to discuss. It also offers a reminder that safe speeds, responsible parking and attention to the road matter long before an accident begins.Disclaimer: This article is based on the supplied incident description and social media reactions. articles.title: Holiday Hunger Bill: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine bill
articles.summary: The education minister has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.
articles.body:
Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food.

The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker.

Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.

The Holiday Meals Payment Bill would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food.

The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday.

Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation.

He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted.

It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal.

As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education.

It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight.

In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it.

He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect.

A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin".

They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands."

articles.title: Fire that killed two sisters was started by candles in flat below
articles.summary: Shikshya and Aanchal Subedi, who were 24 and 28, died in the fire at a block of flats in Aberdeen two years ago.
articles.body:
A fire which killed two sisters in Aberdeen was started by candles in the flat below and spread rapidly, an investigation has found.

Shikshya and Aanchal Subedi, who were 24 and 28, died at the block in the city's Back Hilton Road in January 2024. A joint police and fire investigation was launched into the blaze, but there were no suspicious circumstances found.

It was already known the fire had spread from a neighbouring flat.

A Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) incident report - which has now been obtained by BBC Scotland News through a Freedom of Information (FoI) request - reveals that the fire was started by candles.

The report said a mattress in a lower flat bedroom ignited, and a lithium battery then caused the fire to spread rapidly.

Family asks law firm to investigate blaze that killed two sisters

The report said the victims were already thought to be dead when firefighters got to them, after being trapped by smoke.

The fatal fire on the evening of 29 January 2024 led to a large emergency response.

SFRS sent seven fire engines to the scene as well as specialist resources.

The two sisters originally came from Nepal, but settled in Aberdeen with their family when they were children.

An online fundraiser after their deaths later raised thousands of pounds.

Last month, the family asked a law firm to help a search for answers about the blaze.

Speaking for the first time since losing her younger sisters, Susan Subedi, 35, had said the family still did not know the full facts of what happened two years on.

Susan said: "To say we are devastated doesn't come close to describing how we feel.

"It's very hard to describe how losing Shikshya and Aanchal has affected our family. As sisters we were incredibly close.

"They were only in their 20s, they had everything in life to look forward to but that's been taken away from them and from us."

"We won't laugh or talk or share another family celebration together and sometimes that's too much to bear. I miss them. I will always miss them."

Legal firm Digby Brown said it would seek "all available evidence to help the Subedi family in their pursuit for answers".

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) said it received reports of the deaths of the sisters at the time.

A spokesperson said: "Following a thorough investigation the procurator fiscal concluded that no further action was required."
